facts.statement: Banking Regulation Act (courseware): the wartime period saw expansion of banks with inadequate statutory regulation, unsound practices (indiscriminate opening of branches, employment of unsound methods to attract deposits, interlocking of interests between banks, insurance companies and industrial concerns, dressing up of accounts, dubious devices to become eligible for inclusion in the Second Schedule); the Banking Companies (Inspection) Ordinance and the draft Banking Companies (Restriction of Branches) Bill of 1946 were followed by the Select Committee in November 1946; the Banking Companies Act, 1949 (renamed Banking Regulation Act in 1966) marks an important development, providing statutory directions for the conduct of banks business and its regulation by the Reserve Bank; it made provisions for control over management and an override mechanism and prohibited certain activities. Broad coverage: Part I (short title, extent, commencement; applicable to certain co-operative societies); Part II (forms of business banking companies may engage in, constitution and governance, relative position of the law, minimum paid up capital and reserves, statutory and other requirements, power of the Reserve Bank to give directions, production of documents, inspection and other financial requirements relating to cash reserve; powers to control management: (a) power to remove managerial and other persons from office and (b) power to appoint additional Directors; power of Central Government to acquire undertakings of banking companies in certain cases); Part III (suspension of business and winding up: High Court could act as Court Liquidator and the Reserve Bank as the official Liquidator; the procedure for amalgamation; Part III-A special provisions for speedy disposal of winding up proceedings; Part III-B provisions relating to certain operations of banking companies like powers of central government to make rules relating to the preservation of books, return of paid instruments to customers); Part IV (miscellaneous: penalties, application of fines, change of name); Part V (application of the Act to Co-operative banks). Principal sections: application to all banking companies except primary agricultural credit society and a co-operative society whose primary object and principal business is providing of long-term finance for agricultural purposes (amendment with effect from 26 June 2020); definitions (Sections 5 and 6(1)); prohibition of trade (Sections 8 and 9: non-banking assets disposed within prescribed period); prohibition of employment of managing agents (Section 10); minimum paid up capital and reserves (Section 11); regulation of the proportion of authorised, subscribed and paid up capital and voting rights of shareholders (Section 12); restriction on commission, brokerage, discount on sale of shares and on payment of dividends (Sections 13 to 15); prohibition of common directors among banks (Section 16); Reserve Fund (Section 17); cash reserve by non-scheduled banks (Section 18); restriction on subsidiaries and shareholdings in other companies (Section 19); prohibition of loans on the security of own shares and loans to directors or firms where directors are interested (Section 20); Reserve Bank power to determine policy on advances and give directions (Section 21); licensing of banks (Section 22); licensing of new branches and transfer (Section 23); liquid assets (Sections 24 and 25); return of unclaimed deposits within 30 days of the close of calendar year (Section 26); periodic returns and consolidated information (Sections 27 and 28); balance sheet, audit and publication (Sections 29 to 32); inspection (Section 35); powers to caution or prohibit banks, assist amalgamation, grant loans under Section 18(1)(3) of the RBI Act, and require changes in management (Section 36); annual report on trend and progress of banking in India (Section 36); moratorium, winding up and restrictions on voluntary winding up and amalgamations (Sections 37 to 45); penalties (Sections 46 to 48); application of provisions to the State Bank of India and other notified banks (Section 51); the amendment to Section 18 of the RBI Act to enable the Bank to make loans against security of a bank and first charge on general assets in case of winding up; amendment to Section 42(6) of the RBI Act on inclusion or exclusion of banks from the second schedule (Section 55). The Banking Companies Act repealed Part XA of the Indian Companies Act, 1913 and the Banking Companies (Restriction of Branches) Act, 1946 and the Banking Companies (Inspection) Ordinance, 1946 and the Banking Companies (Control) Ordinance, 1948. The Banking Companies (Amendment) Act of 1950: any scheme of amalgamation had to be approved by a resolution passed by a majority in number representing two-thirds in value of the shareholders present in person or by proxy at a meeting; once sanctioned by the Reserve Bank the scheme would be binding; it also extended the Reserve Bank licensing powers to opening branches outside India.

FEMA and external sector reforms (courseware): the High-Level Committee on Balance of Payments (Chairman: C. Rangarajan, 1993) recommended: (a) introduction of a market-determined exchange rate regime within limits; (b) liberalisation of current account transactions leading to current account convertibility; (c) compositional shift in capital flows away from debt to non-debt flows; (d) strict regulation of external commercial borrowings, especially short-term debt; (e) discouraging volatile elements in flows from non-resident Indians; (f) full freedom for outflows associated with inflows and gradual liberalisation of other outflows; and (g) dissociation of the Government in the intermediation of flow of external assistance. The Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS), a dual exchange rate mechanism, was instituted in March 1992; the dual rate system was a transitional phase culminating in the unified exchange rate system effective from March 1993; India accepted Article VIII of the IMF Articles of Agreement (current account convertibility) in August 1994. The Expert Group on Foreign Exchange Markets (Chairman: O.P. Sodhani) was appointed in November 1994 and submitted its report in June 1995. The Committee on Capital Account Convertibility (CAC; Chairman: S.S. Tarapore) constituted in 1997 sketched a roadmap for achieving capital account convertibility; it spelt out three crucial preconditions: fiscal consolidation, a mandated inflation target and strengthening of the financial system. The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) replaced the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA), 1973 and came into effect from June 2000. The stated objective: to facilitate external trade and payments and promote orderly development and maintenance of foreign exchange markets in India, a shift from conservation of foreign exchange to management; under the new system all genuine current account payments except those notified by the government are eligible for appropriate foreign currency releases from the authorised dealers without any restrictions; the surrender requirements in respect of exports of goods and services continue to operate. The Reserve Bank has regulatory jurisdiction over capital account transactions. Box 5.1: the FEMA provided a de jure status to the external sector policies; unlike FERA, FEMA does not require the prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused person and FEMA provides for appropriate monetary penalty for contraventions; contravention of FEMA provisions are dealt with under civil procedures; administrative mechanisms (Adjudicating Authority, Special Director (Appeals) and Appellate Tribunal) have been provided; the concept of compounding is another distinguishing feature: under FERA all violations were subject to separate investigation and adjudication by the Directorate of Enforcement; under FEMA a contravener can apply for compounding; the compounding authority must dispose of the application within 180 days; the Government designated the Reserve Bank as the compounding authority for all contraventions under FEMA except those involving hawala transactions for which the Directorate of Enforcement would be the compounding authority. The Reserve Bank has delegated considerable powers to authorised dealers to release foreign exchange for a variety of purposes and has been focusing on development of the foreign exchange market with additional hedging instruments such as foreign currency-rupee options, and authorised dealers have been permitted to use innovative products like cross-currency options, interest rate and currency swaps, caps/collars and forward rate agreements (FRAs).

Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 (courseware, as amended up to 1 September 2022): an Ombudsman is an authority appointed to receive and investigate public grievances as a non-adversarial adjudicator. The Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 1995 was framed by the Reserve Bank under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act; the Scheme was modified in 2002 and replaced by the Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006 and later the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021, which integrates the Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006, the Ombudsman Scheme for Non-Banking Financial Companies 2018 and the Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions 2019 (the three repealed); it is framed under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act 1949, Section 45L of the RBI Act 1934 and Section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007, and is focused on cost-free redress of complaints involving deficiency in services rendered by entities regulated by the Reserve Bank if not resolved to the satisfaction of the customers or not replied within a period of 30 days by the regulated entity. In addition, the Scheme also includes under its ambit Non-Scheduled Primary Co-operative Banks with a deposit size of Rs 50 crore and above; the Scheme adopts One Nation One Ombudsman approach by making the RBI Ombudsman mechanism jurisdiction neutral. Features: it is no longer necessary for a complainant to identify under which scheme to file a complaint; deficiency in service is the ground, with a specified list of exclusions, so complaints would no longer be rejected simply on account of not covered under the grounds listed in the scheme; the Scheme has done away with the jurisdiction of each ombudsman office; a Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre at RBI, Chandigarh handles receipt and initial processing of physical and email complaints in any language; the Principal Nodal Officer of the regulated entity will be in the rank of a General Manager in a Public Sector Bank or equivalent; the regulated entity will not have the right to appeal in cases where an Award is issued against it for not furnishing satisfactory and timely information/documents; the Executive Director in charge of the Consumer Education and Protection Department of RBI is the Appellate Authority. The revised Scheme applies to the whole of India to services provided by a regulated entity to its customers under the provisions of the RBI Act 1934, the Banking Regulation Act 1949, the Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007 and the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act 2005. The Reserve Bank may appoint one or more of its officers as Ombudsman and Deputy Ombudsman for a period not exceeding three years at a time. There is no limit on the amount in a dispute that can be brought before the Ombudsman for which the Ombudsman can pass an Award; however, for any consequential loss suffered by the complainant the Ombudsman shall have the power to provide a compensation up to Rupees 20 lakh, in addition to up to Rupees One lakh for the loss of the complainant time, expenses incurred and for harassment/mental anguish suffered. The Ombudsman sends the Deputy Governor a report as on 31 March each year. Any customer aggrieved by an act or omission of a Regulated Entity resulting in deficiency in service may file a complaint personally or through an authorised representative (a person, other than an advocate, duly appointed in writing). Grounds for non-maintainability (the complaint does not lie in matters involving): commercial judgment or decision of a regulated entity; a dispute between a vendor and a regulated entity relating to an outsourcing contract; a grievance not addressed to the Ombudsman directly; general grievances against management or executives; an action initiated in compliance with the orders of a statutory or law enforcing authority; a service not within the regulatory purview of the Reserve Bank; a dispute between regulated entities; a dispute involving the employee-employer relationship; a dispute for which a remedy has been provided in Section 18 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act 2005; and a dispute pertaining to customers not included under the Scheme. A complaint shall not lie unless: the complainant made a written complaint to the regulated entity and (i) the complaint was rejected wholly or partly or the complainant is not satisfied with the reply, or (ii) did not receive any reply within 30 days after the regulated entity received the complaint; the complaint is made to the Ombudsman within one year after the complainant has received the reply from the regulated entity or, where no reply is received, within one year and 30 days from the date of complaint; it is not about the same cause of action already pending or settled before an Ombudsman, Court, Tribunal or Arbitrator; it is not abusive or frivolous or vexatious; the complaint was made to the regulated entity within the period of limitation prescribed under the Limitation Act, 1963; the complainant provides complete information; and the complaint is lodged by the complainant personally or through an authorised representative other than an advocate. Procedure: the complaint may be lodged online through the portal (cms.rbi.org.in) or through the Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre; the regulated entity files its written version with copies of documents within 15 days of receipt of the copy of the complaint; an ex-parte order may be passed if it fails to do so; the complaint is deemed resolved when it has been settled with the complainant on the intervention of the Ombudsman, the complainant has agreed in writing or otherwise that the manner and the extent of resolution is satisfactory, or the complainant has withdrawn the complaint voluntarily; the Ombudsman may also award a compensation not exceeding Rs 1 lakh; the Award shall lapse and be of no effect unless the complainant furnishes a letter of acceptance of the Award in full and final settlement of the claim within a period of 30 days from the date of receipt of the copy of the Award; the Regulated Entity shall comply with the Award within 30 days from the date of receipt of the letter of acceptance from the complainant, unless it has preferred an appeal. The complaint may be rejected by the Deputy Ombudsman or the Ombudsman at any stage if it appears the complaint is non-maintainable or is in the nature of offering suggestions or seeking guidance or explanation, or there is no deficiency in service, or the compensation sought for consequential loss is beyond the power of the Ombudsman. Appeals: the Regulated Entity aggrieved by an Award may within 30 days from the date of receipt of communication of Award prefer an appeal before the Appellate Authority (with the previous sanction of the Chairman or Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer or in their absence the Executive Director/Official of equal rank; the Appellate Authority may allow a further period not exceeding 30 days on sufficient cause); the complainant aggrieved by an Award or rejection may within 30 days from receipt prefer an appeal before the Appellate Authority; the Appellate Authority may dismiss the appeal, allow it and set aside the Award, remand the matter to the Ombudsman for fresh disposal, modify the Award or pass any other order. The Principal Nodal Officer of the regulated entity at its head office shall not be of rank less than a General Manager or equivalent. Banks must display the contact details of the Banking Ombudsman in all offices and branches, the scheme copy must be available in the premises and be displayed on websites, and appoint Nodal Officers at Regional/Zonal Offices.

Financial sector reforms (courseware): in the 1980s financial markets were highly segmented and controlled; interest rates in the government securities and credit markets were tightly regulated; the banking sector was dominated by public sector banks with a significant quantum of non-performing assets; credit was extended to the Government by mandating a minimum Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) whereby commercial banks had to invest substantial portions of their liabilities in government securities at below market interest rates. Pre-reform, the banking system witnessed positive developments in geographical spread of branches and functional coverage, but there were also major adverse developments: the system saddled with a large volume of non-performing assets and faced several challenges in not being very efficient. Macro-economic crisis in early 1991: weak with rising inflation, high fiscal deficit, low economic growth and unsustainable current account deficit in the wake of the Gulf war and precipitated into a balance of payments crisis; by August 1991 inflation had reached a peak of 17 per cent on an annualised basis; foreign exchange reserves had adequate level reached a negligible level. The Government of India launched several stabilisation and structural adjustment measures: stabilisation of the economy so that balance of payments and inflationary pressures were kept under control; deregulation of the real and financial sectors and removal of licence and permit system; liberalisation of international trade; globalisation to attract international capital and modern technology. The Financial Sector Reforms Committee (Chairman: M. Narasimham) was appointed in 1992; the first phase of reforms guided by its recommendations aimed at enhancing the operational flexibility and financial autonomy of banks with a view to fostering efficiency, productivity and profitability; later the Government appointed the second committee on Banking Sector Reforms (Narasimham Committee-II) with the objective of focusing on strengthening the foundations of the banking system; based on its recommendations the second phase of reforms was implemented. The first phase focused on deregulation of the banking industry including permitting the entry of new private sector banks, measures to strengthen the institutional framework in banking, non-banking financial institutions and capital markets through introduction of prudential norms, capital adequacy stipulations, improvements in payments and settlement systems and strengthening of the supervisory framework; institutional measures included the setting up of the Board for Financial Supervision for strengthening the Bank supervisory mechanism, recapitalisation of banks and improvements in debt recovery procedures and processes. The second phase focused on the banking system with an emphasis on the prudential aspects: prudential norms conforming to international standards have been gradually introduced; steps taken to increase the capital adequacy ratio; assign risk weights to Government approved securities to take care of market risk; assign risk weights to open positions in forex and gold; the stipulated level of capital adequacy on account of implementing the recommendations of Narasimham Committee II warranted a substantial infusion of capital into the banking system; income recognition norms: income on assets must not be recognised if not received within two quarters after it is past the period due (i.e. due date plus ninety days) namely the 90 day delinquency norm; a decision related to treatment of assets guaranteed by the State Government as non-performing under certain circumstances. Recovery of debts: banks and financial institutions experienced considerable difficulties in recovering loans; the Committee on the Financial System headed by Shri Narasimham had considered the setting up of Special Tribunals with special powers for adjudication of such matters and speedy recovery as critical to the successful implementation of financial sector reforms; in 1981 a committee under the Chairmanship of Shri T. Tiwari had examined the legal and other difficulties faced by banks and financial institutions and suggested remedial measures including setting up of special tribunals; consequently the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions (DRT) Act 1993 was enacted; the Government constituted thirty-three Debts Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) and five Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunals (DRATs) across the country; the Debts Recovery Tribunal enforces provisions of the RDDBFI Act 1993 and also the SARFAESI Act 2002; the fundamental purpose of the 1993 Act was to remove claims of banks and financial institutions from the ordinary form of recovery to specialised tribunals; under RDDBFI Act 1993 banks approach the DRT whereas under SARFAESI Act 2002 borrowers, guarantors and any other person aggrieved by any action of the bank can approach the DRT; appeals against orders passed by DRT lie before the DRAT; each DRT is presided over by a Presiding Officer; each DRT has two Recovery Officers. A bill to amend the SARFAESI Act 2002 etc. was introduced (the Enforcement of Security Interest and Recovery of Debt Laws and Miscellaneous Provisions (Amendment) Bill, 2016) to amend four acts: SARFAESI Act 2002, RDDBFI Act 1993, the Indian Stamp Act 1899 and the Depositories Act 1996; Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs): the bill gives the Reserve Bank powers to audit and inspect ARCs; the RBI Master Circular of 10 February 2022 directed fit and proper criteria for sponsors of ARCs; reforms in other segments: the Development Finance Institutions (DFIs) were brought under the regulation of the RBI; the insurance sector remained in public ownership until the late 1990s, then the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDA) Act 1999; the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) was established as the regulator in February 1992; the monopoly of Unit Trust of India (UTI) ended in 1992 when mutual funds were opened to the private sector; Indian companies were allowed to tap international capital markets through ADRs, GDRs, FCCBs and ECBs; FIIs were permitted to invest in all types of securities including Government securities with full capital convertibility. Debt market reforms: the Reserve Bank entered into a historic agreement with the Government in September 1994 for gradual phasing out of ad hoc treasury bills; ad hoc Treasury Bills were discontinued from April 1, 1997; the Government Securities Act, 2006 repealed the Public Debt Act, 1944 and came into force from 1 December 2007; interest rates on Government paper have been made market related; since April 1992 the Central Government borrowing programme has been conducted largely through auctions enabling market based price discovery; LAF was introduced: an interim adjustment facility in 1999 with (a) export refinance to commercial banks, (b) collateralised lending facility (CLF), (c) additional collateralised lending facility (ACLF) to scheduled commercial banks, and (d) liquidity support at two levels to Primary Dealers; the Narasimham Committee II recommendations led to a full-fledged LAF implemented in stages from June 2000 and May 2001; CBLO operationalised by CCIL on January 2003 and replaced by Tri-party Repo from 5 November 2018 (courseware states 5.11.2018 although another unit gives 10 August 2017); the minimum maturity period of Certificate of Deposits was reduced from 15 days to 7 days effective April 2005. Outcomes: GDP growth of around 6.4 per cent in 1995-96 to 2000-01; inflation brought down to 5 per cent by end-March 2001; fiscal deficit 5.1 per cent of GDP in 2000-01; capital inflows maintained a healthy trend and foreign exchange reserves of US$ 42.3 billion in March 2001.

Other financial regulators and division of functions (courseware): the financial system comprises distinct segments (banking, insurance, capital market) each regulated by specialised authorities; the structure should ensure the soundness of the entire system. Four broad approaches to financial supervision and regulation: institutional supervision (supervision is performed over each single category of financial institution, and each such function is assigned to a distinct agency; the traditional approach); supervision by objectives (each single authority is responsible for one objective of regulation regardless of the legal form of intermediaries); functional supervision (considers the economic functions performed in the financial system as given); and single regulator supervision (one control authority with responsibility over all markets and intermediaries regardless of whether banking, financial or insurance). The superiority of one model over the other has proved to be inconclusive. Global experience indicates that in most cases the function of supervision of banks is performed very effectively by central banks; in the UK, the FSA-type single agency model was in place (the courseware notes it is difficult to judge). In India, the broad approach followed corresponds to the institutional based system of regulation: the Reserve Bank acts as a supervisory body for banks, NBFCs and all-India financial institutions (AIFIs); the Registrar of Co-operatives (ROC) of different States is a joint regulator for the banks in the co-operative sector, both urban and rural; SEBI regulates the capital markets and several financial institutions such as stock exchanges, mutual funds and other asset management companies, securities dealers and brokers, merchant bankers and credit rating agencies; the insurance sector is regulated by Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDA). Regulatory overlaps: the duality of control over the banking system between the Reserve Bank and the Banking Division, Ministry of Finance should end and the Reserve Bank should be the primary agency for regulation of the banking system; the need to establish a Super Regulator to supervise and coordinate the activities of multiple regulators in order to ensure uniformity in regulatory treatment was brought out by the Khan Working Group; the need for greater coordination in regulation through the High Level Group on Capital Markets by conferring a legal status to it was emphasised by the Deepak Parekh Group; it was proposed that the BFS continue to supervise banks and non-banks with a Deputy Governor as Chairman, IRDA should supervise insurance and SEBI continue its regulatory jurisdiction over capital market; the apex financial regulatory authority may be constituted by statute with the Governor of the Reserve Bank as Chairman and the members could be the Chairmen of the three regulatory agencies; the High Level Coordination Committee on Financial and Capital Markets (HLCC) is headed by the Governor of the Reserve Bank, with Finance Secretary, Chairman SEBI and Chairman IRDA as members, and has set up three Technical Standing Committees (on the banking sector, the insurance sector and the capital market) to review developments; the courseware concludes that regulatory overlaps and conflicts on turf grounds and regulatory arbitrage are negligible.

Institutions set up by the Reserve Bank (courseware): one of the primary tasks of central banks in developing countries is to build a well-differentiated institutional credit structure; the Reserve Bank agricultural credit: the All-India Rural Credit Survey Committee (Chairman: A.D. Gorwala, 1951); its recommendations (Committee of Direction report 1954) led to the nationalisation of the Imperial Bank of India (SBI, 1955) and restructuring of the short-term co-operative credit structure; the Agricultural Credit Department; the RBI Act amended in 1955 to enable the Bank to create two funds: National Agricultural Credit (Long-Term Operations) Fund and National Agricultural Credit (Stabilisation) Fund; the Agricultural Refinance Corporation set up in 1963 for extending medium and long-term finance to agriculture and renamed the Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation in 1975 (courseware); NABARD set up on July 12, 1982 as an apex refinancing institution for agriculture and rural development combining developmental and financial roles; the Rural Planning and Credit Cell (set up 1979; CRAFICARD) was renamed; after nationalisation the Reserve Bank financial inclusion roles continued. NABARD: initial capital Rs 100 crore contributed equally by the Union Government and the RBI, with a proviso to raise it later to Rs 500 crore (capital has since been raised to Rs 2,000 crore); the entire assets and liabilities of ARDC were also taken over by NABARD; for short-term operations it is entitled to funds mainly from the RBI and for its long-term loans, it draws funds from the Central Government, floats bonds in the open market and also draws from the two National Rural Credit Funds; main function: refinance, credit for promotion of agriculture, small-scale and cottage industries, handicrafts and other rural crafts and other allied activities in rural areas; short-term credit (repayable within 18 months) by way of refinance to State Co-operative Banks and RRBs; medium-term loans 3 to 7 years and long-term up to 25 years; the RRBs and Co-operative sector now come under the supervisory purview of the NABARD. IDBI: constituted under the Industrial Development Bank of India Act, 1964 as a wholly owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India to give impetus to industrial growth, on July 1, 1964; apex institution; de-linked from the RBI in February 1976 and made an autonomous corporation with the Government as owner; authorised capital Rs 50 crore (later raised to Rs 200 crore); four roles: coordinating agency, financing agency, refinancing agency and an agency promoting industrial development; transformed into a Bank under the Industrial Development Bank (Transfer of Undertaking and Repeal) Act, 2003, with the Industrial Development Bank of India Ltd incorporated on 27 September 2004, transferring the undertaking from October 1, 2004; the name changed to IDBI Bank Limited from 7 May 2008. DFHI (Discount and Finance House of India): established in April 1988 following the Vaghul Committee (Working Group on Money Market) recommendations by the Reserve Bank jointly with public sector banks and financial institutions with an authorised capital of Rs 250 crore; the RBI later offloaded part of its holdings; the major objective: to facilitate the smoothening of imbalances in short-term liquidity by developing an active secondary market for money market instruments and integrate the segments of the money market; deals in Treasury Bills, Commercial Bills, Certificates of Deposit and Commercial Paper; commenced dealing in Government of India dated securities from April 1992; authorised as a Primary Dealer from February 29, 1996; now known as SBIDFHI. IRBI: set up in April 1971 as the Industrial Reconstruction Corporation of India (IRCI), reconstituted as the Industrial Reconstruction Bank of India in 1985 under the IRBI Act, 1984 as a principal credit and reconstruction agency for industrial revival, modernisation, rehabilitation. UTI: established in February 1964 as a Trust under the UTI Act 1963 to mobilise the savings of small investors for industrial development and give small investors a share in profits of industry; an associate institute of RBI until 1976 when it was made an associate institute of IDBI; the UTI Act was repealed after the 2001 crisis, the UTI was bifurcated into two parts: UTI Mutual Fund and the Specified Undertaking of UTI (SUUTI). EXIM Bank: established on 1 January 1982 under the Export-Import Bank of India Act, 1981, taking over export financing functions of the IDBI; the premier export finance institution; lines of credit to overseas financial institutions and foreign governments, Overseas Investment Finance, export marketing finance, Rural Initiatives Programme and Export Marketing Services. NHB: set up on 9 July 1988 under the National Housing Bank Act 1987 (the Bill passed in winter session of 1987 and received assent on 23 December 1987) as a wholly owned subsidiary of the RBI, an apex institution for housing finance; the Head Office is in New Delhi; it contributed to the entire paid-up capital; objectives: to promote a sound, healthy, viable and cost effective housing finance system; a network of dedicated housing finance institutions; augment resources; make housing credit more affordable; regulate and supervise housing finance companies (the regulatory functions of HFCs have been taken over by the RBI); encourage supply of buildable land and building materials; the Rangarajan High-Level Group led to the NHB. CCIL: set up in April 2001 for exclusive clearing and settlement for transactions in Money, Government Securities and Foreign Exchange; commenced operations on 15 February 2002 when the Negotiated Dealing System (NDS) went live; CBLO launched in January 2003; forex trading platform FX-CLEAR (live 7 August 2003); cross-currency settlement through CLS Bank from 6 April 2005; manages NDS-OM and NDS-CALL. BCSBI: the Reserve Bank constituted the Committee on Procedures and Performance Audit of Public Services under S.S. Tarapore in November 2003; the Banking Codes and Standards Board of India was set up in 2006 as an autonomous independent watchdog registered as a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, dissolved with effect from 28 September 2021 (courseware). NPCI: the Reserve Bank released a vision document incorporating a proposal to set up an umbrella institution for all the retail payment systems; National Payments Corporation of India incorporated in December 2008 as a Section 25 company with the Certificate of Commencement of Business issued in April 2009; the authorised capital Rs 300 crore and paid-up capital Rs 60 crore; NPCI has ten promoter banks; BPSS in-principle approval on September 24, 2008 to operate NFS ATM network; NPCI took over NFS from IDRBT; services: Cheque Clearing, IMPS (24x7x365), Automated Clearing House, Electronic Benefit Transfer and RuPay card; UPI launched by NPCI built on IMPS, using Virtual Payment Address (VPA); other mobile methods use account number with IFSC, mobile number with MMID, Aadhaar, MPIN. NARCL (National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited): incorporated under the Companies Act and granted an ARC licence by the Reserve Bank; capitalised through equity contributions from banks and financial institutions; it will initially acquire NPAs with total secured outstanding exposure of Rs 500 crore and above amounting to about Rs 2 lakh crore; following extant guidelines it would acquire these assets through 15 per cent upfront payment in cash and 85 per cent in security receipts (SRs); the SRs issued will be guaranteed by the government to cover the difference between the face value of SRs and actual realisation from the resolution process for up to five years; an amount of Rs 30,600 crore has been earmarked for the purpose; PSBs and government owned FIs will hold a minimum of 51 per cent stake. NaBFID (National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development): Government has paved the way for the establishment of a development financial institution through enactment of the National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development Act; Union Budget 2021-22 budgeted Rs 20,000 crores for it; NaBFID is the fifth AIFI besides Exim Bank, NABARD, NHB and SIDBI. Risk thresholds for the Prompt Corrective Action framework for NBFCs (Table 5.1): regulatory minimum CRAR 15 per cent (Threshold I: 12 per cent but less than 15 per cent; Threshold II: 9 per cent but less than 12 per cent; Threshold III: below 9 per cent); Tier I capital regulatory minimum 10 per cent (Threshold I: 8 per cent but less than 10 per cent; II: 6 per cent but less than 8 per cent; III: below 6 per cent); Net NPA ratio: Threshold I more than 6 per cent but less than or equal to 9 per cent; II more than 9 per cent but less than or equal to 12 per cent; III higher than 12 per cent; leverage ratio regulatory minimum 2.5 times (Threshold I: 2.5 times but less than 3 times; II: 3 times but less than 3.5 times; III: greater than 3.5 times).

payload.title: The Banking Regulation Act: need, coverage and principal sections
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Why it was needed (wartime banking):** **indiscriminate branch opening**, **unsound deposit-attracting methods**, **interlocking** of banks with **insurance and industrial concerns**, **dressing up of accounts** and **dubious devices** to enter the **Second Schedule**. The **Banking Companies Act, 1949** (renamed **Banking Regulation Act in 1966**) gave **statutory direction** to banking business and its **regulation by the Reserve Bank**, including **control over management** and an **override mechanism**.

**Five parts:**

- **Part I:** short title, extent, commencement (also certain **co-operative societies**).
- **Part II:** **forms of business**, constitution and governance, **minimum capital and reserves**, cash reserve, the Reserve Bank's **directions, inspection** and **control over management** (**remove managerial persons, appoint additional directors**, **Government acquisition of undertakings**).
- **Part III:** **suspension of business and winding up** (High Court, **court liquidator**, Reserve Bank as **official liquidator**), **III-A** speedy winding up, **III-B** records and returning paid instruments.
- **Part IV:** **penalties, fines, change of name**.
- **Part V:** application to **co-operative banks**.

**Principal sections (courseware list):** **5 and 6(1)** definitions and forms of business; **8-9** no trade, **non-banking assets** disposed within the **prescribed period**; **10** no **managing agents** or commission-paid staff; **11** minimum **paid-up capital and reserves**; **12** capital proportions and **voting rights**; **13-15** commission, **unpaid capital**, **dividends**; **16** no **common directors**; **17** **reserve fund**; **18** **cash reserve** (non-scheduled banks); **19** **subsidiaries**; **20** no **loans on own shares or to directors**; **21** **directions on advances**; **22** **licensing**; **23** **branches**; **24-25** **liquid assets**; **26** **unclaimed deposits** (**30 days** after the calendar year); **27-28** **returns**; **29-32** **balance sheet, audit**; **35** **inspection**; **36** **caution, prohibition, assistance with amalgamation**, **annual report on Trend and Progress**; **37-45** **moratorium, winding up, amalgamation**; **46-48** **penalties**; **51** **SBI and other notified banks**; **55** amendment of **RBI Act Sections 18 and 42(6)**.

**1950 amendment:** an **amalgamation scheme** needs a **majority in number representing two-thirds in value** of **each bank's shareholders**, then **Reserve Bank sanction**; it also gave the Reserve Bank **licensing power over branches abroad**. The Act repealed **Part XA of the Indian Companies Act 1913**, the **1946 Branches and Inspection** measures and the **1948 Control Ordinance**.

payload.title: FEMA and the external sector reforms
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Rangarajan High-Level Committee on Balance of Payments (1993):** a **market-determined exchange rate within limits**; **current account convertibility**; **shift from debt to non-debt flows**; **strict regulation of external commercial borrowings (short-term debt)**; **discourage volatile NRI flows**; **free outflows tied to inflows** and gradual freedom for others; **end Government intermediation of external assistance**.

**Milestones:** **LERMS** (dual rate) **March 1992**; **unified market rate from March 1993**; **Article VIII of the IMF Articles accepted in August 1994** (current account convertibility); **Sodhani Expert Group** (**November 1994**, report **June 1995**) on the forex market; **Tarapore Committee on Capital Account Convertibility (1997)**, which set **three preconditions**: **fiscal consolidation**, a **mandated inflation target** and **strengthening the financial system**.

**FEMA, 1999 (effective June 2000)** replaced **FERA, 1973**: from **conservation** to **management** of foreign exchange; **genuine current account payments** (except notified items) are released by **authorised dealers** without restriction; **surrender of export proceeds** continues; the RBI controls **capital account transactions**.

**Differences from FERA (Box 5.1):** **civil**, not criminal, treatment: the prosecution **need not prove guilt**; **monetary penalties**; an **Adjudicating Authority, Special Director (Appeals) and Appellate Tribunal**; **compounding**: a contravener may apply, and the **compounding authority must decide within 180 days**; the **Reserve Bank** is the compounding authority for all contraventions **except hawala**, where the **Directorate of Enforcement** is.

**Market development:** wide delegation to **authorised dealers**; **options, cross-currency options, swaps, caps/collars and FRAs**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: FEMA shifted foreign exchange law from prohibition to facilitation, backed by civil penalties and compounding.

payload.title: The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021: scope, maintainability and procedure
payload.core_explanation_md:
**What it is:** a **cost-free redress** mechanism for **deficiency in service** by **regulated entities**, under **Section 35A (BR Act)**, **Section 45L (RBI Act)** and **Section 18 (PSS Act)**. It **integrates** the **Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006**, the **NBFC Ombudsman Scheme 2018** and the **Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions 2019** (**all repealed**); it also covers **non-scheduled primary co-operative banks with deposits of Rs 50 crore and above**; **One Nation One Ombudsman** (**jurisdiction neutral**).

**Features:** the complainant **need not name the scheme**; **deficiency in service** is the ground with a list of **exclusions**; **no territorial jurisdiction per office**; a **Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre, Chandigarh**; the regulated entity's **Principal Nodal Officer** is a **General Manager** (or equivalent) at **head office**; the **Appellate Authority** is the **Executive Director in charge of the Consumer Education and Protection Department**; an entity **cannot appeal** an Award issued because it **did not give satisfactory information on time**.

**Awards:** no cap on the **amount in dispute**; compensation for **consequential loss up to Rs 20 lakh** plus **up to Rs 1 lakh** for **time, expenses, harassment and mental anguish** (courseware, dated). The Ombudsman is an **RBI officer** appointed for **up to three years**; an **annual report** goes to the **Deputy Governor** as on **31 March**.

**Complaint is not maintainable** for: **commercial judgment** of the entity; **vendor outsourcing disputes**; a grievance **not addressed to the Ombudsman directly**; **general grievances against management**; **action under orders of a statutory or law enforcing authority**; services **outside RBI purview**; disputes **between regulated entities**; **employer-employee disputes**; a remedy under **Section 18 of the CIC Act**; customers not covered.

**A complaint lies only if:** the complainant first **complained in writing to the entity** and the reply was **rejected or unsatisfactory** or **no reply came in 30 days**; the complaint reaches the Ombudsman **within one year** of the reply (or **one year and 30 days** from the complaint if no reply); it is **not pending or decided elsewhere** (Ombudsman, court, tribunal, arbitrator); **not frivolous or abusive**; the first complaint was within **Limitation Act** time; the complainant gives **complete information**; and it is lodged **personally or by an authorised representative who is not an advocate**.

**Procedure:** file **online (cms.rbi.org.in)** or via the **Centralised Centre**; the entity files its **written version within 15 days**; failing which the Ombudsman may pass an **ex-parte order**. **Resolution:** **settlement**, **complainant's agreement** or **withdrawal**. An **Award** **lapses unless accepted in 30 days** and the entity **complies within 30 days of acceptance** unless it appeals. **Appeals:** the **entity** (with **prior sanction of the CMD/CEO or ED**) or the **complainant** within **30 days** (up to **30 more** on cause); the **Appellate Authority** may **dismiss, allow, remand, modify** or pass other orders. Banks must **display** the **Ombudsman's contact details** and the **Scheme**, appoint **Nodal Officers** at regional and zonal offices and a **Principal Nodal Officer**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Scheme gives customers a free, single-window route when a regulated entity does not resolve a complaint.

payload.title: Financial sector reforms after 1991
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Before reform (1980s):** **segmented, controlled markets**, **regulated rates**, **public sector bank dominance with high NPAs**, and **SLR** forcing banks to lend to the Government at **below-market rates**.

**1991 crisis:** high **inflation (peak 17 per cent annualised in August 1991)**, high **fiscal deficit**, low growth, an **unsustainable current account deficit** (Gulf war) and a **balance of payments crisis**. **Response:** **stabilisation**, **deregulation** (end of licence-permit), **liberalisation of trade**, **globalisation**.

**Narasimham Committee on the Financial System (1991-92):** **first phase** (**deregulation**, **new private banks**, **prudential norms**, **capital adequacy**, **payment systems**, **Board for Financial Supervision**, **recapitalisation**, **debt recovery**); **Committee II** led to a **second phase** (**prudential aspects**: **risk weights for government securities** and **forex and gold open positions**, **higher capital adequacy**, the **90 day delinquency norm** for income recognition, **State-guaranteed assets** to be treated as NPA in some cases).

**Debt recovery:** the **Tiwari Committee (1981)** and Narasimham proposed **special tribunals**; the **RDDBFI Act, 1993** created **Debts Recovery Tribunals** and **Appellate Tribunals** (the courseware says **33 DRTs and 5 DRATs**); each DRT has a **Presiding Officer** and **two Recovery Officers**. Banks go to the DRT under the **RDDBFI Act**, while under **SARFAESI (2002)** **borrowers and others aggrieved by a bank action** go to the DRT. The **2016 Amendment Bill** changed the **SARFAESI, RDDBFI, Indian Stamp and Depositories Acts**; **ARCs** are subject to RBI **audit and inspection** and **fit and proper** criteria for sponsors (**Master Circular of 10 February 2022**).

**Other segments:** **DFIs** and **NBFCs** under RBI regulation; **IRDA Act 1999** (insurance opened); **SEBI (1992)**; **UTI** monopoly ended **1992**; **ADRs, GDRs, FCCBs, ECBs**; **FII** access with **full capital convertibility**.

**Debt market reforms:** **September 1994** agreement to phase out **ad hoc Treasury Bills** (**discontinued from 1 April 1997**); **Government Securities Act, 2006** (**in force from 1 December 2007**) **replaced the Public Debt Act, 1944**; **market-related rates** and **auctions since April 1992**; **LAF**: an **interim facility in 1999** (export refinance, **CLF**, **ACLF**, **PD liquidity support**) and **full LAF in stages from June 2000 and May 2001**; **CBLO** (CCIL, **January 2003**) later replaced by **tri-party repo**; **CD minimum maturity cut from 15 to 7 days** (**April 2005**).

**Outcomes (dated):** growth about **6.4 per cent**, inflation about **5 per cent**, fiscal deficit **5.1 per cent of GDP** and reserves **US$ 42.3 billion** (**March 2001**).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The reforms replaced administered controls with prudential norms, market pricing and legal recovery tools.

payload.title: Other financial regulators and the division of functions
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Four approaches to supervision:**

| Approach | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Institutional** | Each **category of institution** has its own supervisor (traditional) |
| **By objectives** | Each authority handles **one objective** (for example **prudential** or **conduct**) across institutions |
| **Functional** | Supervision follows the **economic function**, whatever the institution |
| **Single regulator** | **One authority** for **all markets and intermediaries** (the **UK FSA** model) |

No model is clearly superior; **most countries** keep **bank supervision in the central bank**.

**India (institutional model):** the **Reserve Bank** supervises **banks, NBFCs and all-India financial institutions**; the **Registrar of Co-operatives (State)** is a **joint regulator** of **co-operative banks**; **SEBI** regulates **capital markets** (stock exchanges, mutual funds, brokers, merchant bankers, rating agencies); **IRDA** regulates **insurance**.

**Overlap and coordination:** the **Khan Working Group** argued for a **Super Regulator** and the **Deepak Parekh Group** for **legal status** for the **High Level Coordination Committee on Financial and Capital Markets (HLCC)**, chaired by the **Governor** with the **Finance Secretary** and the **Chairmen of SEBI and IRDA**, with **three Technical Standing Committees** (banking, insurance, capital markets). Other views: the **duality of control** between the Reserve Bank and the **Banking Division, Ministry of Finance** should end; an **apex regulatory authority** chaired by the **Governor** could coordinate. The courseware concludes that **regulatory overlaps and arbitrage are small** and that the Indian model works with **coordination**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: India has several specialised regulators coordinated by a high-level committee rather than a single super regulator.

items.title: The Banking Regulation Act: need, coverage and principal sections
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why it was needed (wartime banking):** **indiscriminate branch opening**, **unsound deposit-attracting methods**, **interlocking** of banks with **insurance and industrial concerns**, **dressing up of accounts** and **dubious devices** to enter the **Second Schedule**. The **Banking Companies Act, 1949** (renamed **Banking Regulation Act in 1966**) gave **statutory direction** to banking business and its **regulation by the Reserve Bank**, including **control over management** and an **override mechanism**.

**Five parts:**

- **Part I:** short title, extent, commencement (also certain **co-operative societies**).
- **Part II:** **forms of business**, constitution and governance, **minimum capital and reserves**, cash reserve, the Reserve Bank's **directions, inspection** and **control over management** (**remove managerial persons, appoint additional directors**, **Government acquisition of undertakings**).
- **Part III:** **suspension of business and winding up** (High Court, **court liquidator**, Reserve Bank as **official liquidator**), **III-A** speedy winding up, **III-B** records and returning paid instruments.
- **Part IV:** **penalties, fines, change of name**.
- **Part V:** application to **co-operative banks**.

**Principal sections (courseware list):** **5 and 6(1)** definitions and forms of business; **8-9** no trade, **non-banking assets** disposed within the **prescribed period**; **10** no **managing agents** or commission-paid staff; **11** minimum **paid-up capital and reserves**; **12** capital proportions and **voting rights**; **13-15** commission, **unpaid capital**, **dividends**; **16** no **common directors**; **17** **reserve fund**; **18** **cash reserve** (non-scheduled banks); **19** **subsidiaries**; **20** no **loans on own shares or to directors**; **21** **directions on advances**; **22** **licensing**; **23** **branches**; **24-25** **liquid assets**; **26** **unclaimed deposits** (**30 days** after the calendar year); **27-28** **returns**; **29-32** **balance sheet, audit**; **35** **inspection**; **36** **caution, prohibition, assistance with amalgamation**, **annual report on Trend and Progress**; **37-45** **moratorium, winding up, amalgamation**; **46-48** **penalties**; **51** **SBI and other notified banks**; **55** amendment of **RBI Act Sections 18 and 42(6)**.

**1950 amendment:** an **amalgamation scheme** needs a **majority in number representing two-thirds in value** of **each bank's shareholders**, then **Reserve Bank sanction**; it also gave the Reserve Bank **licensing power over branches abroad**. The Act repealed **Part XA of the Indian Companies Act 1913**, the **1946 Branches and Inspection** measures and the **1948 Control Ordinance**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Act turned scattered rules into a single law of banking regulation under the Reserve Bank.

items.title: FEMA and the external sector reforms
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rangarajan High-Level Committee on Balance of Payments (1993):** a **market-determined exchange rate within limits**; **current account convertibility**; **shift from debt to non-debt flows**; **strict regulation of external commercial borrowings (short-term debt)**; **discourage volatile NRI flows**; **free outflows tied to inflows** and gradual freedom for others; **end Government intermediation of external assistance**.

**Milestones:** **LERMS** (dual rate) **March 1992**; **unified market rate from March 1993**; **Article VIII of the IMF Articles accepted in August 1994** (current account convertibility); **Sodhani Expert Group** (**November 1994**, report **June 1995**) on the forex market; **Tarapore Committee on Capital Account Convertibility (1997)**, which set **three preconditions**: **fiscal consolidation**, a **mandated inflation target** and **strengthening the financial system**.

**FEMA, 1999 (effective June 2000)** replaced **FERA, 1973**: from **conservation** to **management** of foreign exchange; **genuine current account payments** (except notified items) are released by **authorised dealers** without restriction; **surrender of export proceeds** continues; the RBI controls **capital account transactions**.

**Differences from FERA (Box 5.1):** **civil**, not criminal, treatment: the prosecution **need not prove guilt**; **monetary penalties**; an **Adjudicating Authority, Special Director (Appeals) and Appellate Tribunal**; **compounding**: a contravener may apply, and the **compounding authority must decide within 180 days**; the **Reserve Bank** is the compounding authority for all contraventions **except hawala**, where the **Directorate of Enforcement** is.

**Market development:** wide delegation to **authorised dealers**; **options, cross-currency options, swaps, caps/collars and FRAs**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: FEMA shifted foreign exchange law from prohibition to facilitation, backed by civil penalties and compounding.

items.title: The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021: scope, maintainability and procedure
items.core_explanation_md:
**What it is:** a **cost-free redress** mechanism for **deficiency in service** by **regulated entities**, under **Section 35A (BR Act)**, **Section 45L (RBI Act)** and **Section 18 (PSS Act)**. It **integrates** the **Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006**, the **NBFC Ombudsman Scheme 2018** and the **Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions 2019** (**all repealed**); it also covers **non-scheduled primary co-operative banks with deposits of Rs 50 crore and above**; **One Nation One Ombudsman** (**jurisdiction neutral**).

**Features:** the complainant **need not name the scheme**; **deficiency in service** is the ground with a list of **exclusions**; **no territorial jurisdiction per office**; a **Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre, Chandigarh**; the regulated entity's **Principal Nodal Officer** is a **General Manager** (or equivalent) at **head office**; the **Appellate Authority** is the **Executive Director in charge of the Consumer Education and Protection Department**; an entity **cannot appeal** an Award issued because it **did not give satisfactory information on time**.

**Awards:** no cap on the **amount in dispute**; compensation for **consequential loss up to Rs 20 lakh** plus **up to Rs 1 lakh** for **time, expenses, harassment and mental anguish** (courseware, dated). The Ombudsman is an **RBI officer** appointed for **up to three years**; an **annual report** goes to the **Deputy Governor** as on **31 March**.

**Complaint is not maintainable** for: **commercial judgment** of the entity; **vendor outsourcing disputes**; a grievance **not addressed to the Ombudsman directly**; **general grievances against management**; **action under orders of a statutory or law enforcing authority**; services **outside RBI purview**; disputes **between regulated entities**; **employer-employee disputes**; a remedy under **Section 18 of the CIC Act**; customers not covered.

**A complaint lies only if:** the complainant first **complained in writing to the entity** and the reply was **rejected or unsatisfactory** or **no reply came in 30 days**; the complaint reaches the Ombudsman **within one year** of the reply (or **one year and 30 days** from the complaint if no reply); it is **not pending or decided elsewhere** (Ombudsman, court, tribunal, arbitrator); **not frivolous or abusive**; the first complaint was within **Limitation Act** time; the complainant gives **complete information**; and it is lodged **personally or by an authorised representative who is not an advocate**.

**Procedure:** file **online (cms.rbi.org.in)** or via the **Centralised Centre**; the entity files its **written version within 15 days**; failing which the Ombudsman may pass an **ex-parte order**. **Resolution:** **settlement**, **complainant's agreement** or **withdrawal**. An **Award** **lapses unless accepted in 30 days** and the entity **complies within 30 days of acceptance** unless it appeals. **Appeals:** the **entity** (with **prior sanction of the CMD/CEO or ED**) or the **complainant** within **30 days** (up to **30 more** on cause); the **Appellate Authority** may **dismiss, allow, remand, modify** or pass other orders. Banks must **display** the **Ombudsman's contact details** and the **Scheme**, appoint **Nodal Officers** at regional and zonal offices and a **Principal Nodal Officer**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Scheme gives customers a free, single-window route when a regulated entity does not resolve a complaint.

items.title: Financial sector reforms after 1991
items.core_explanation_md:
**Before reform (1980s):** **segmented, controlled markets**, **regulated rates**, **public sector bank dominance with high NPAs**, and **SLR** forcing banks to lend to the Government at **below-market rates**.

**1991 crisis:** high **inflation (peak 17 per cent annualised in August 1991)**, high **fiscal deficit**, low growth, an **unsustainable current account deficit** (Gulf war) and a **balance of payments crisis**. **Response:** **stabilisation**, **deregulation** (end of licence-permit), **liberalisation of trade**, **globalisation**.

**Narasimham Committee on the Financial System (1991-92):** **first phase** (**deregulation**, **new private banks**, **prudential norms**, **capital adequacy**, **payment systems**, **Board for Financial Supervision**, **recapitalisation**, **debt recovery**); **Committee II** led to a **second phase** (**prudential aspects**: **risk weights for government securities** and **forex and gold open positions**, **higher capital adequacy**, the **90 day delinquency norm** for income recognition, **State-guaranteed assets** to be treated as NPA in some cases).

**Debt recovery:** the **Tiwari Committee (1981)** and Narasimham proposed **special tribunals**; the **RDDBFI Act, 1993** created **Debts Recovery Tribunals** and **Appellate Tribunals** (the courseware says **33 DRTs and 5 DRATs**); each DRT has a **Presiding Officer** and **two Recovery Officers**. Banks go to the DRT under the **RDDBFI Act**, while under **SARFAESI (2002)** **borrowers and others aggrieved by a bank action** go to the DRT. The **2016 Amendment Bill** changed the **SARFAESI, RDDBFI, Indian Stamp and Depositories Acts**; **ARCs** are subject to RBI **audit and inspection** and **fit and proper** criteria for sponsors (**Master Circular of 10 February 2022**).

**Other segments:** **DFIs** and **NBFCs** under RBI regulation; **IRDA Act 1999** (insurance opened); **SEBI (1992)**; **UTI** monopoly ended **1992**; **ADRs, GDRs, FCCBs, ECBs**; **FII** access with **full capital convertibility**.

**Debt market reforms:** **September 1994** agreement to phase out **ad hoc Treasury Bills** (**discontinued from 1 April 1997**); **Government Securities Act, 2006** (**in force from 1 December 2007**) **replaced the Public Debt Act, 1944**; **market-related rates** and **auctions since April 1992**; **LAF**: an **interim facility in 1999** (export refinance, **CLF**, **ACLF**, **PD liquidity support**) and **full LAF in stages from June 2000 and May 2001**; **CBLO** (CCIL, **January 2003**) later replaced by **tri-party repo**; **CD minimum maturity cut from 15 to 7 days** (**April 2005**).

**Outcomes (dated):** growth about **6.4 per cent**, inflation about **5 per cent**, fiscal deficit **5.1 per cent of GDP** and reserves **US$ 42.3 billion** (**March 2001**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The reforms replaced administered controls with prudential norms, market pricing and legal recovery tools.

items.title: Other financial regulators and the division of functions
items.core_explanation_md:
**Four approaches to supervision:**

| Approach | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Institutional** | Each **category of institution** has its own supervisor (traditional) |
| **By objectives** | Each authority handles **one objective** (for example **prudential** or **conduct**) across institutions |
| **Functional** | Supervision follows the **economic function**, whatever the institution |
| **Single regulator** | **One authority** for **all markets and intermediaries** (the **UK FSA** model) |

No model is clearly superior; **most countries** keep **bank supervision in the central bank**.

**India (institutional model):** the **Reserve Bank** supervises **banks, NBFCs and all-India financial institutions**; the **Registrar of Co-operatives (State)** is a **joint regulator** of **co-operative banks**; **SEBI** regulates **capital markets** (stock exchanges, mutual funds, brokers, merchant bankers, rating agencies); **IRDA** regulates **insurance**.

**Overlap and coordination:** the **Khan Working Group** argued for a **Super Regulator** and the **Deepak Parekh Group** for **legal status** for the **High Level Coordination Committee on Financial and Capital Markets (HLCC)**, chaired by the **Governor** with the **Finance Secretary** and the **Chairmen of SEBI and IRDA**, with **three Technical Standing Committees** (banking, insurance, capital markets). Other views: the **duality of control** between the Reserve Bank and the **Banking Division, Ministry of Finance** should end; an **apex regulatory authority** chaired by the **Governor** could coordinate. The courseware concludes that **regulatory overlaps and arbitrage are small** and that the Indian model works with **coordination**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: India has several specialised regulators coordinated by a high-level committee rather than a single super regulator.

items.core_explanation_md:
**Agriculture and rural credit:** the **All-India Rural Credit Survey (Gorwala, 1951)** led to the **Imperial Bank's nationalisation (SBI, 1955)**; the **1955 RBI Act amendment** created the **National Agricultural Credit (Long-Term Operations) and (Stabilisation) Funds**; **Agricultural Refinance Corporation (1963)** became **ARDC** and then **NABARD** (**12 July 1982**): **initial capital Rs 100 crore** (Government and RBI equally); **short-term refinance** (up to **18 months**), **medium term (3-7 years)** and **long term (up to 25 years)**; the **RRBs and co-operatives** now fall under **NABARD supervision**.

**Industry and finance institutions:**

| Institution | Key facts (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **IDBI** | **IDBI Act 1964**; set up **1 July 1964** as an **RBI subsidiary**; **de-linked in February 1976**; four roles (**coordinating, financing, refinancing, promotional**); became a **bank** under the **2003 Repeal Act** (**IDBI Ltd incorporated 27 September 2004**; **IDBI Bank Ltd from 7 May 2008**) |
| **DFHI** | **April 1988**, after the **Vaghul Committee**; secondary market for **money market instruments** (T-bills, commercial bills, CDs, CP); **dated securities from April 1992**; **Primary Dealer from 29 February 1996**; now **SBIDFHI** |
| **IRBI** | **IRCI (April 1971)** → **IRBI (1985, IRBI Act 1984)**: **reconstruction and rehabilitation** of **sick industry** |
| **UTI** | **Trust under the UTI Act 1963**, **February 1964**; **RBI associate until 1976**, then IDBI; **bifurcated after 2001**: **UTI Mutual Fund** and **SUUTI** |
| **EXIM Bank** | **1 January 1982**, **Export-Import Bank of India Act 1981**; took over IDBI's **export financing**; **lines of credit** abroad, **Overseas Investment Finance**, **export marketing** |
| **NHB** | **9 July 1988**, **National Housing Bank Act 1987** (Presidential assent **23 December 1987**); **RBI wholly owned**; **Rangarajan group**; apex for **housing finance**; **HFC regulation moved to the RBI** |
| **CCIL** | **April 2001**; clearing and settlement for **money, G-secs and forex**; **NDS live 15 February 2002**; **CBLO January 2003**; **FX-CLEAR 7 August 2003**; **CLS settlement from 6 April 2005**; runs **NDS-OM and NDS-CALL** |
| **BCSBI** | **2006**, a **self-regulatory** society (**Tarapore Committee 2003** recommendation); **dissolved from 28 September 2021** (courseware) |
| **NPCI** | **Incorporated December 2008** (Section 25 company; **commencement April 2009**); **umbrella for retail payments**; **NFS (taken over from IDRBT)**, **IMPS, ACH, EBT, RuPay**, **UPI** (built on IMPS using a **Virtual Payment Address**) |
| **NARCL** | An **ARC** capitalised by banks and FIs; buys NPAs of **Rs 500 crore and above** for **15 per cent cash and 85 per cent security receipts** guaranteed by Government (dated figures not taught); **PSBs and Government-owned FIs hold at least 51 per cent** |
| **NaBFID** | Development finance institution for **infrastructure**, the **fifth AIFI** after **Exim, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI** |

**PCA for NBFCs (Table 5.1):** thresholds for **CRAR (15 per cent regulatory minimum)**, **Tier I (10 per cent)**, **net NPA** and **leverage** (dated table, not taught).
